verses.text: "I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard.
He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful.
You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you.
Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me.
I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.
If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away and withers. Such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burned.
If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.
This is to My Father's glory, that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples.
As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love.
If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love, just as I have kept My Father's commandments and remain in His love.
I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete.
This is My commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends.
You are My friends if you do what I command you.
No longer do I call you servants, for a servant does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you.
You did not choose Me, but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain—so that whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you.
This is My command to you: Love one another.
If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first.
If you were of the world, it would love you as its own. Instead, the world hates you, because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world.
Remember the word that I spoke to you: 'No servant is greater than his master.' If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well; if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well.
But they will treat you like this because of My name, since they do not know the One who sent Me.
If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not be guilty of sin. Now, however, they have no excuse for their sin.
Whoever hates Me hates My Father as well.
If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin; but now they have seen and hated both Me and My Father.
But this is to fulfill what is written in their Law: 'They hated Me without reason.'
When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father—He will testify about Me.
And you also must testify, because you have been with Me from the beginning.

context.author: Traditionally the apostle John
context.genre: Theological narrative — a continuation of Jesus' farewell discourse, built around a single extended image (the vine) followed by warnings about coming opposition
context.audience: A broad, likely mixed Jewish and Gentile readership toward the end of the first century
context.setting: Spoken the night before the crucifixion, most likely after the meal and on the way toward Gethsemane (14:31; 18:1). The disciples had just walked past the temple, whose entrance was famously decorated with a massive golden vine symbolizing Israel — a striking backdrop for Jesus calling Himself the "true" vine.
context.custom: Vineyards covered the Judean hillsides, and pruning was a familiar annual task — cutting away dead wood and also trimming healthy shoots so the vine's strength went into fruit rather than leaves. The golden vine on Herod's temple, described by the historian Josephus, had clusters of grapes as large as a person, donated in gold leaf by wealthy Jews as a symbol of national identity.
context.timelineImmediate: This chapter continues the unbroken night-before-the-cross conversation, shifting from the comfort of chapter 14 toward a sober preparation: the disciples are told both how to stay fruitful in Him and what hostility to expect from the world once He is gone.
context.timelineBible: The Old Testament repeatedly pictures Israel as God's vine, almost always as a failure — Isaiah 5 describes a vine that yielded only wild grapes. By calling Himself the "true" vine, Jesus claims to be everything Israel was meant to be, the one who actually produces what God was looking for.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus calls Himself the true vine, the Father the vinedresser, and His followers the branches, with one repeated command: remain connected, because apart from Him they can do nothing. The same chapter moves from fruitfulness into love — the disciples are called friends rather than servants, and told to love each other as He loved them. It closes with a sober warning that the world that hated Him will hate them too, balanced by the promise of the Spirit who will testify alongside them.

translation.meaning: Also translated "abide" in older versions — it means to stay put, to keep on, to dwell. The word appears over forty times in John's Gospel, and eleven times in this one short chapter, making it the central idea of the passage.

The verb means to cleanse or clean, and it sits right beside the word for "clean" in the very next verse (katharoi) — a deliberate wordplay linking the Father's pruning with the cleansing that has already been done through Jesus' word.

Jesus draws a clear line between a servant, who simply carries out orders without knowing the reasons, and a friend, who has been told the whole purpose. What makes the disciples friends is that He has made everything He learned from the Father known to them.

otBackground.note: Israel as God's vineyard that produced only wild grapes — the failure Jesus' claim to be the "true" vine answers.
Israel pictured as a vine brought out of Egypt and planted by God.
"They hated me without reason" — the verses Jesus says are fulfilled in the world's hatred of Him.

commentary.note: Henry reads "true" as the opposite of counterfeit: Christ is not like the wild vine in 2 Kings 4:39 that poisoned those who gathered from it, but a real, fruitful plant — the one that Judah's vine in Genesis 49:11 and Joseph's vine in Genesis 49:22 only pointed toward. He also notes it reflects Christ's humility that He chose such a low, ordinary comparison for Himself.

On "apart from Me you can do nothing," Henry makes a practical point: being fruitful matters so much to our happiness that it becomes the strongest reason to stay connected to Christ — "the best argument to engage us to abide in Christ is, that otherwise we cannot be fruitful." On friends versus servants, he adds that those who do a servant's duty are advanced to a friend's dignity.

Guzik reads the branches that are "taken away" as ones that were never truly abiding, shown by the fact that they bore no fruit — and presses the emphasis plainly: "there are no true disciples who do not abide." A branch only has life as long as it stays connected to the vine, the same way disciples only live spiritually when connected to the Master.
